IRD Pathology Lab

Learning objectives

  1. LO 1Match each layer of normal skin to how it looks under the microscope, and name the cells and cell junctions that live in each layer.
  2. LO 2For acne, eczematous (atopic) dermatitis and psoriasis: explain what drives each one, what it looks like on the skin and on biopsy, and how it is treated first.
  3. LO 3Tell pemphigus vulgaris apart from bullous pemphigoid by the patient, the blister, the level of the split on biopsy and the immunofluorescence pattern.
  4. LO 4For basal cell carcinoma, keratoacanthoma, squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma: know who gets them, how they look grossly and under the microscope, and which genes drive them.

MAPBig picture

  • Know normal skin first → every lesion = a change at one level
    • corneum → parakeratosis · spinosum → spongiosis / acantholysis · BM → subepidermal split · basale → BCC, melanoma
  • Acne → plugged follicle + androgens + C. acnes → inflamed papule / pustule / cyst → retinoid + antimicrobial
  • Eczema → red, weeping, itchy rash → spongiosis → CD4 T cells (type IV) → topical steroids
    • atopic → filaggrin · atopic triad
  • Psoriasis → silvery plaques on extensors → T cells → TNF / IL-12 / IL-17 → turnover 28 d → 3–4 d
    • parakeratosis · long rete · no granular layer · neutrophils · Auspitz
  • Blisters → level of split decides the disease
    • PV → anti-desmoglein → suprabasal → flaccid → net IF · mouth first
    • BP → anti-BPAG → subepidermal → tense → linear IF · elderly
  • Neoplasms → UV is the shared driver
    • keratinocyte → BCC (palisading, PTCH1) · KA (crater, regresses) · SCC (keratin, invades)
    • melanocyte → melanoma (ABCDE, depth = prognosis, BRAF)

LO 1Normal skin histologyThe layers, their cells and the junctions that hold them together

By the end: you can label a low- and high-power image of normal skin, list the epidermal layers outer → inner with one key feature each, name which junction sits where, and use the basic lesion and histology vocabulary that the rest of this lab depends on.
Q1. At low power, what are the three layers of skin and what lives in the dermis?
  • Three layers, outer → inner: epidermis → dermis → subcutaneous tissue (loose connective tissue + fat).
  • On top of the epidermis is a thin keratin layer.
    • Keratin is thicker on palms and soles and anywhere skin is chronically rubbed or irritated.
  • Dermis = connective tissue with collagen + elastic fibers, in two zones:
    • Papillary dermis (superficial, touches epidermis) → small capillaries for temperature regulation.
    • Reticular dermis (deeper) → mostly dense, glassy pink collagen.
  • Adnexa you will see in the dermis:
    • Hair follicle with surrounding sebaceous glands (pale, bubbly cells; empty sebum into the follicle → the unit that plugs in acne).
    • Arrector pili = small bundle of smooth muscle attached to the follicle → contracts with cold or stress → hair "stands on end" and skin dimples = goose bumps.
CheckOn a low-power image, a pale cluster of foamy, lipid-filled cells sits beside a hair shaft, and a thin pink band of spindle cells runs diagonally from the follicle. Name both.
Foamy cells = sebaceous gland; pink spindle-cell band = arrector pili (smooth muscle).
Q2. What are the epidermal layers, outer → inner, and what identifies each one?
LayerWhat you seeWhy it matters
Stratum corneumAcellular keratin (dead keratinocytes, no nuclei); continually desquamates; thickest in thick skinNuclei retained here = parakeratosis (fast turnover → psoriasis)
Stratum lucidumThin, darker red / clear band just under the corneum; 2–3 cells thick; thick skin only (palms, soles)Nearly indistinguishable in most biopsies
Stratum granulosum3–5 cell layers of flattened, diamond-shaped cells with purple cytoplasmic granulesKeratohyalin granules (filaggrin → bundles keratin) + lamellar granules that secrete glycolipid "glue" (water barrier). Lost in psoriasis
Stratum spinosumThickest layer (8–10 cells); polyhedral cells with intercellular bridges ("prickle cells")Bridges = desmosomes → target in pemphigus vulgaris; edema here = spongiosis; thickening = acanthosis
Stratum basaleSingle row of cuboidal → columnar stem cells (highest mitotic activity) + melanocytes (brown melanin)Anchored to the basement membrane by hemidesmosomes → target in bullous pemphigoid; origin of BCC and melanoma
CheckWhich epidermal layer is present on the sole of the foot but absent from the skin of the back?
Stratum lucidum (thick skin only).
CheckWhich layer has the purple granules, and what do they do?
Stratum granulosum: keratohyalin granules (filaggrin bundles keratin) and lamellar granules that release lipid "glue" for the water barrier.
Q3. Which cells and junctions matter for the diseases in this lab?

Keratinocytes

  • Born in the basale → mature upward → die as keratin
  • Normal transit basale → surface ≈ 28 days (~1 month)
  • Joined to each other by desmosomes (cadherins = desmogleins)

Melanocytes

  • Sit in the stratum basale
  • Make melanin → transfer it to nearby keratinocytes
  • Melanin = natural sunscreen (brown basal pigment on H&E)

Basal cell anchors

  • Basale → hemidesmosomes → basement membrane → dermis
  • Hemidesmosome proteins = BPAG1 / BPAG2
Desmosomekeratinocyte ↔ keratinocyte (spinosum)
→
Attackedanti-desmoglein IgG
→
Pemphigus vulgarissplit inside epidermis
Hemidesmosomebasal cell ↔ BM
→
Attackedanti-BPAG IgG + C3
→
Bullous pemphigoidsplit below epidermis
CheckA basal cell loses its grip on the basement membrane, but keratinocytes stay stuck to each other. Which junction failed?
Hemidesmosomes (BPAG1/2) → the pattern of bullous pemphigoid.
Q4. What vocabulary do I need to describe skin lesions and skin biopsies?

Clinical lesion terms (10 mm cut-off)

Type<10 mm>10 mm
Flat discolorationMaculePatch
Raised, solidPapulePlaque
Fluid-filledVesicleBulla
Deeper, larger massNodule (dermis / subcutis)
Tissue lossErosion (upper epidermis) vs ulcer (into dermis)
SurfaceScale = piled-up stratum corneum

Histology terms

  • Hyperkeratosis → thick stratum corneum
  • Parakeratosis → nuclei kept in the stratum corneum (↑ turnover)
  • Acanthosis → thickened epidermis (spinosum), not the corneum
  • Spongiosis → edema fluid between keratinocytes → intraepidermal vesicles
  • Acantholysis → keratinocytes lose their connections to each other
  • Dysplasia / atypia → large, dark, irregular nuclei; loss of orderly maturation

A good skin history asks: onset and triggers, first site and spread, family history of atopy, occupational exposures, sun exposure, travel, and medications.

CheckA biopsy shows a thick layer of keratin, but every flake still contains a small dark nucleus. Which two terms apply?
Hyperkeratosis (thick corneum) with parakeratosis (retained nuclei).
Step 1 HY
  • Junction → disease: desmosome (desmoglein) → pemphigus vulgaris; hemidesmosome (BP180/BPAG2) → bullous pemphigoid.
  • Melanocytes come from the neural crest (stain S-100). Langerhans cells (dendritic APCs with Birbeck granules) sit in the spinosum.
  • Filaggrin (from keratohyalin) loss-of-function → atopic dermatitis, ichthyosis vulgaris.
Step 1 trap

Acanthosis ≠ hyperkeratosis. Acanthosis = a thicker epidermis (more spinosum). A thick stratum corneum is hyperkeratosis; a thick corneum with nuclei is parakeratosis. Psoriasis has all three, which is why they get blurred together.

Memory tool

Layers outer → inner: "Come, Let's Get Sun Burned" → Corneum, Lucidum, Granulosum, Spinosum, Basale.

Desmosome = detween cells (PV); hemidesmosome = half on the cell, half on the BM (BP).

Buzzwords
"prickle cells" → stratum spinosum"purple granules" → granulosum"goose bumps" → arrector pili"retained nuclei in keratin" → parakeratosis

ApplyLO 1 application questions

A1A biopsy from the palm shows a thick acellular keratin layer with a thin bright-red band beneath it. Why is that band missing on a biopsy from the abdomen?
It is the stratum lucidum, found only in thick skin. Palms and soles are thick skin; the abdomen is thin skin.
A2Predict what happens if a toxin dissolves desmosomes but spares hemidesmosomes.
Keratinocytes separate from each other within the epidermis (acantholysis) while basal cells stay on the BM. The result is an intraepidermal blister, like pemphigus.
A3A patient has a 2-cm raised, solid, scaly lesion. Use the correct lesion term.
Plaque with scale. Raised and solid; plaque because it is >10 mm; scale = piled-up corneum.
A4In which layer would you expect most mitoses in normal epidermis, and which pigment-producing cell sits there too?
Stratum basale; melanocytes. The basale holds the stem cells (most mitotic activity) and the melanocytes.

LO 2Acne, eczema and psoriasisPathogenesis, clinical look, biopsy findings and first-line treatment

By the end: you can explain the acne cascade, recognize eczema by spongiosis and its type IV mechanism, list the psoriasis biopsy findings (parakeratosis, regular acanthosis, long rete, lost granular layer, neutrophils), and pick the first-line treatment for each.
Q1. How does acne form, and what does it look like grossly and on biopsy?
Puberty↑ androgens → ↑ sebum (sebaceous hypertrophy)
→
Plugsebum + keratin block the follicle → comedone
→
BacteriaCutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes lipases → irritating fatty acids
→
Inflammationpapule → pustule → nodule
→
Rupturecyst >0.5 cm into dermis → scarring
  • Types: open comedones (blackheads) · closed comedones (whiteheads) · inflammatory papules/pustules · nodulocystic (severe).
  • Gross: scattered red inflammatory papules and occasional pustules (face, back).
  • Who: nearly all teens after puberty to some degree. Usually self-limited, but 10–20% of adults keep having acne.
    • Boys > girls; may persist longer in young women; scarring more likely in men.
  • Biopsy (severe lesion): low power is dominated by marked acute (neutrophils) and chronic inflammation filling the dermis around a ruptured, keratin-plugged follicle; it looks "blurry blue" at low power because of all the inflammatory cells.
  • Treatment: topical retinoid (vitamin A derivative) + antimicrobial.
CheckWhy does a bacterium that lives harmlessly on everyone's skin drive acne inflammation?
Inside a plugged follicle it has plenty of sebum; its lipases break lipids into irritating free fatty acids that trigger inflammation.
Step 1 HY
  • Severe nodulocystic acne → oral isotretinoin: highly teratogenic (needs two forms of contraception, pregnancy tests); also dry skin, ↑ triglycerides.
  • Acne flaring with hirsutism or irregular menses → think PCOS / androgen excess.
Memory tool

Acne = 4 Ps: Puberty hormones, Plugged follicle, Propionibacterium, Pus (inflammation).

Q2. What is eczema, how does it look, and what is the mechanism?
  • Eczema = generic clinical term for a red, itchy, papulovesicular eruption that can ooze ("weep"), crust and scale.
    • Forms: allergic contact, atopic, drug-induced, photo-, irritant dermatitis, insect-bite reactions.
    • Gross: a nonspecific red rash (e.g., on a leg) with fine papules and crust.
  • Key biopsy finding = spongiosis: edema fluid collects between keratinocytes within the epidermis → forms vesicles.
    • At low power the fluid looks like multiple round "balls" / bubbles scattered inside the epidermis.
    • Dermis: edema (loose, pale spaces) with a lymphocytic infiltrate, sometimes with eosinophils (bright pink granules).
    • Chronic itching → scratching → acanthosis (thickened epidermis).
  • Mechanism: type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity
    • First exposure to antigen (chemicals in plants, drugs, manufactured products) → memory T cells.
    • Re-exposure → CD4 T cells recruited → release cytokines → inflammation.
    • Classic contact dermatitis appears 24–72 h (1–3 days) after exposure.
  • Reading the infiltrate: a lymphocyte-rich picture points to the type IV (T-cell) mechanism; when eosinophils are prominent, the question is pointing at the IgE / type I (allergic, atopic) component.

Atopic dermatitis specifically

Why it happens

  • Multifactorial: genetics + skin barrier dysfunction + environmental triggers + delayed hypersensitivity
  • Filaggrin mutations → skin cannot stay moist
  • Part of the atopic triad: atopic dermatitis + allergic asthma + allergic rhinoconjunctivitis
  • Major symptom = itching

Where it shows up

  • Infants: cheeks, scalp, extensor surfaces
  • Children: flexural creases, neck, elbows
  • Adults: hands, wrists, forehead, around eyes
  • Treatment: topical corticosteroids
CheckA hiker develops an itchy, weeping, linear rash 2 days after a walk through brush. Which cell drives it, and what is the hallmark biopsy finding?
CD4 T cells (type IV, delayed); biopsy shows spongiosis with intraepidermal vesicles.
Step 1 HY
  • Contact dermatitis classics: poison ivy (urushiol), nickel (jewelry, belt buckles), neomycin, latex; patch test = type IV.
  • Atopic dermatitis = Th2 / IgE plus barrier defect (filaggrin); ↑ serum IgE, eosinophilia; colonized by S. aureus.
  • Boards phrase eczema histology as "spongiotic dermatitis".
Step 1 trap

Spongiosis vs acantholysis. Both put fluid in the epidermis. Spongiosis = many round edema pools, cells still connected by stretched bridges (eczema). Acantholysis = cells detached, one long split above the basal row (pemphigus).

Buzzwords
"weeping, crusted, itchy" → eczema"24–72 h after contact" → type IV"flexural creases + asthma" → atopic dermatitis"filaggrin" → barrier defect
Q3. What drives psoriasis, and how do you recognize it?
  • Who: 1–2% of people, all ages. Autoimmune / inflammatory and multi-organ.
    • About two-thirds carry HLA-Cw*0602.
    • Associated: psoriatic arthritis (can resemble RA), spondylitis, myopathy; nail pitting and brownish discoloration.
  • Pathogenesis:
    T cellsCD4 ↔ epidermal dendritic cells ↔ CD8
    →
    CytokinesTNF · IL-12 · IL-17 · IFN-γ
    →
    Keratinocyteshyperproliferate + inflammation
    →
    Turnover~28 days → 3–4 days → scale builds up
  • Gross: well-demarcated pink plaque with thick silvery scale over bony prominences (elbows, knees), scalp, genitalia, hands; itchy, sometimes painful.
  • Biopsy (the in-house list):
    • Parakeratosis (nuclei in the stratum corneum).
    • Regular acanthosis (evenly thickened epidermis) with downward elongation of rete ridges = elongated dermal papillae in between.
    • Thinning / loss of the stratum granulosum; thin suprapapillary plates.
    • Collections of neutrophils in the epidermis/corneum: Munro microabscesses and spongiform pustules.
    • Dilated capillaries in the papillae, right under the surface → lifting the scale tears them = pinpoint bleeding = Auspitz sign.
  • Treatment: holistic primary + subspecialty care (topicals → systemic / biologic agents aimed at the cytokines above).
CheckWhy does scraping a psoriatic plaque cause pinpoint bleeding?
Dilated capillaries in elongated dermal papillae sit just under thinned suprapapillary plates; removing the scale tears them (Auspitz sign).
Q4. How do I tell acne, eczema and psoriasis apart on a biopsy?
FeatureAcne vulgarisEczemaPsoriasis
GrossPapules, pustules, comedones on face/backRed, weeping, crusted, itchy rashSilvery-scaled plaques on extensors, scalp
Biopsy clueDense acute + chronic inflammation through dermis around a ruptured follicleSpongiosis (round intraepidermal fluid pools); dermal lymphocytes ± eosinophilsParakeratosis, regular acanthosis, long rete, no granular layer, neutrophils in epidermis
DriverAndrogens, sebum, keratin plug, C. acnesCD4 T cells (type IV); atopic: filaggrin, IgET cells → TNF, IL-12, IL-17, IFN-γ; HLA-Cw*0602
First-line TxTopical retinoid + antimicrobialTopical corticosteroidsTopicals → systemic / biologics
CheckBiopsy: neutrophil clusters inside a thick, nucleated corneum. Eczema or psoriasis?
Psoriasis: Munro microabscesses in parakeratotic scale. Eczema is lymphocyte-rich with spongiosis.
Step 1 HY
  • Psoriasis biologics map to the cytokines: anti-TNF (etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab), anti-IL-12/23 (ustekinumab), anti-IL-17A (secukinumab, ixekizumab).
  • Koebner phenomenon: plaques appear at sites of trauma.
  • Psoriatic arthritis: DIP joints, dactylitis ("sausage digits"), "pencil-in-cup" X-ray.
Step 1 trap

Location sorts the rashes: psoriasis = extensor (elbows, knees); atopic dermatitis in children/adults = flexor creases. Infant eczema is the exception (extensors, cheeks).

Memory tool

Psoriasis biopsy = "Pink PANTS": Parakeratosis, Acanthosis (regular), Neutrophils (Munro), Thin plates + no granular layer, Stretched (long) rete with dilated capillaries.

Buzzwords
"silvery scale on extensors" → psoriasis"Auspitz sign" → psoriasis"Munro microabscess" → psoriasis"nail pitting" → psoriasis"HLA-Cw6" → psoriasis

ApplyLO 2 application questions

A1A 17-year-old has comedones and inflamed papules on his back. His mother asks why topical antibiotics are part of the plan. What do you say?
They reduce C. acnes, whose lipases make inflammatory fatty acids in plugged follicles. The retinoid treats the plug; the antimicrobial treats the bacterial driver of inflammation.
A2A woman gets an itchy, oozing rash on her wrist 2 days after wearing a new metal bracelet. Biopsy mechanism?
Type IV hypersensitivity (CD4 memory T cells) → spongiosis. Allergic contact dermatitis (nickel) appears 24–72 h after re-exposure.
A3A 5-year-old with asthma has chronic itchy, lichenified patches in the elbow creases. Which gene defect, and what first-line treatment?
Filaggrin loss → barrier dysfunction; topical corticosteroids. Atopic triad (eczema, asthma, allergic rhinitis) with flexural distribution in a child.
A4Predict the effect of a drug that blocks IL-17 on psoriatic plaques, and why.
Plaques thin and clear. IL-17 (with TNF, IL-12, IFN-γ) drives keratinocyte hyperproliferation; blocking it slows the 3–4-day turnover back toward normal.
A5A biopsy shows thick nucleated scale, absent granular layer and long, evenly spaced rete ridges. Name the gross lesion you expect.
Well-demarcated plaque with silvery scale (psoriasis) on elbows, knees or scalp.

LO 3Pemphigus vulgaris vs bullous pemphigoidTwo autoimmune blistering diseases split at different levels

By the end: you can explain why the level of the split predicts whether a blister is flaccid or tense, give the target antigen and immunofluorescence pattern of each disease, and separate eczema, pemphigus and pemphigoid on a low-power biopsy.
Q1. Why do blisters form at different levels, and why does it matter?
  • Both diseases are autoimmune: IgG autoantibodies attack an adhesion protein → cells come apart → fluid fills the gap → blister.
  • The level of the split decides the roof, and the roof decides the bulla:
    • Subcorneal (just under the corneum) → roof = corneum only (pemphigus foliaceus).
    • Suprabasal (just above the basal layer) → roof = most of the epidermis, basal cells stay on the floor (pemphigus vulgaris).
    • Subepidermal (below the whole epidermis) → roof = entire epidermis (bullous pemphigoid).
  • Rule: thin, intraepidermal roof → flaccid, ruptures easily; full-thickness roof → tense, stays intact.
CheckWhich blister would you expect to still find intact at the bedside: suprabasal or subepidermal? Why?
Subepidermal: its roof is the full-thickness epidermis, so the bulla is tense and resists rupture.
Q2. What are the features of pemphigus vulgaris?

Clinical PV

Adults 30–60 (often 50s–60s). Flaccid vesicles and bullae that rupture easily → shallow erosions covered with dried serum and crust.

Oral mucosal erosions in most patients, often months before skin lesions. Sites: scalp, face, axillae, groin, trunk, pressure points.

Pathogenesis

IgG against desmoglein 1 and 3 (desmosomes that bind keratinocytes) → cells detach (acantholysis); binding also activates proteases that destroy adhesion further.

Anti-Dsg3 alone → mucosal-only disease; anti-Dsg1 correlates more with prognosis. Circulating antibody can be measured.

Biopsy + IF

Suprabasal acantholytic blister within the epidermis: one long, straight cleft just above the basal layer; basal cells stay on the BM ("tombstones").

Direct IF: intercellular IgG between keratinocytes → net-like ("chicken-wire") pattern.

Treatment + outcome

Corticosteroids halt progression; immunosuppressants for maintenance. Aggressive and can be fatal untreated; mortality up to 15%, partly from immunosuppression complications.

CheckOn low power, how does the fluid in pemphigus vulgaris differ from the fluid in eczema?
PV: one long, straight split just above the basal layer. Eczema: multiple round fluid "balls" scattered within the epidermis (spongiosis).
Q3. What are the features of bullous pemphigoid?

Clinical BP

Older adults. Large tense bullae filled with clear fluid (can reach several cm) that do not rupture easily; often pruritic.

Flexural skin: axillae, groin, inner thighs, flexor forearms, lower abdomen. Oral lesions only 10–15%, and they follow the skin lesions. Ruptured bullae leave pink, hive-like areas.

Pathogenesis

Triggers: drugs, infections, physical trauma, systemic disease.

IgG against BPAG1 and BPAG2 (hemidesmosomes anchoring basal cells to the BM) → complement fixation → recruits inflammatory cells; ↑ IL-16 (CD4 chemotaxis) and matrix metalloproteinases.

Biopsy + IF

Subepidermal, non-acantholytic blister: intact epidermis lifted off the dermis. Infiltrate with fibrin, lymphocytes, eosinophils (just under the epidermis), neutrophils; edematous superficial dermis.

Direct IF: linear IgG + C3 along the basement membrane.

Treatment + outcome

Anti-inflammatory / immunosuppressive therapy; remission after months to years. Usually heals without scarring. Generalized bullous form is most common.

CheckWhich inflammatory cell, sitting just below the epidermis, is a strong clue to bullous pemphigoid?
Eosinophils (with fibrin and lymphocytes) in a subepidermal blister.
Q4. Side by side: how do I separate them (and eczema) fast?
FeaturePemphigus vulgarisBullous pemphigoid
PatientAdults 30–60Older adults (often >70)
BullaeFlaccid, rupture → crusted erosionsTense, rarely rupture; itchy
Oral mucosaMost, often first~10–15%, after skin
SplitSuprabasal, acantholyticSubepidermal, non-acantholytic
InfiltrateSparseEosinophils, lymphocytes, neutrophils, fibrin
Direct IFIntercellular, net-like IgGLinear IgG + C3 along BM
TargetDesmoglein 1/3 (desmosome)BPAG1/2 (hemidesmosome)
CourseAggressive; mortality up to 15%Milder; heals without scarring

Three-way histology sort

EczemaPemphigus vulgarisBullous pemphigoid
Where is the fluid?Within epidermis, between cellsJust above the basal layerBelow the entire epidermis
Low-power lookMany round bubblesOne long straight cleftWhole epidermis lifted off
MechanismSpongiosis (edema)AcantholysisHemidesmosome loss
Step 1 HY
  • Nikolsky sign: positive in PV (skin shears off with lateral pressure), negative in BP.
  • Both are type II hypersensitivity (antibody against a fixed tissue antigen).
  • BP antigen on boards = BP180 (BPAG2, collagen XVII); PV = desmoglein 3 (± 1).
Step 1 trap
  • Dermatitis herpetiformis is also subepidermal, but IF shows granular IgA in dermal papillae and it comes with celiac disease. Linear IgG = BP.
  • Pemphigus foliaceus: anti-Dsg1, subcorneal, crusted scales, no mucosal involvement.
Memory tool

PV = Vulnerable, Very fragile roof, mouth first (Vocal/oral). BP = Below the epidermis, Bullae stay Big and tense, Basement-membrane line.

IF: pemphigus = fishnet; pemphigoid = pencil line.

Buzzwords
"tombstone basal cells" → PV"chicken-wire IF" → PV"oral erosions first" → PV"elderly, tense, itchy bullae" → BP"linear IgG/C3 at BM" → BP"eosinophils under epidermis" → BP

ApplyLO 3 application questions

A1A 52-year-old has had painful mouth sores for 4 months and now has crusted erosions on his scalp and trunk; intact blisters are hard to find. Predict the biopsy and IF.
Suprabasal acantholytic blister; net-like intercellular IgG. Pemphigus vulgaris: flaccid bullae rupture, oral disease comes first.
A2An 81-year-old nursing-home resident started a new drug 3 weeks ago and now has itchy, tense bullae on his inner thighs; mouth is clear. Target antigen?
BPAG2 (and BPAG1) in hemidesmosomes. Bullous pemphigoid; drugs are a recognized trigger.
A3Serum from a patient with only oral erosions is tested for antibodies. Which desmoglein is the antibody most likely against?
Desmoglein 3. Anti-Dsg3 alone → mucosal-only disease; adding anti-Dsg1 brings skin involvement and tracks with prognosis.
A4A biopsy shows multiple round, clear spaces scattered through the middle of the epidermis with lymphocytes in the dermis. A classmate calls it pemphigus. Correct them.
It is spongiosis (eczema). Pemphigus shows a single long suprabasal cleft with detached (acantholytic) cells, not multiple round edema pools.

LO 4Skin neoplasmsBCC, keratoacanthoma, SCC and melanoma: risks, gross, micro and genes

By the end: you can sort the four tumors by cell of origin, name each one's risk factors and driver genes, recognize each grossly and on biopsy (including SCC in situ and the two faces of melanoma), and state the key prognostic factor for melanoma.
Q1. How are skin cancers grouped, and what do they have in common?

Keratinocyte-derived

  • Basal cell carcinoma (most common)
  • Keratoacanthoma (low-grade squamous)
  • Squamous cell carcinoma (2nd most common)

Melanocyte-derived

  • Melanoma: less common, but causes most skin-cancer deaths (high metastatic potential)
  • Presentation: often asymptomatic; head/neck lesions found earlier because they are visible.
    • A red or pigmented lesion that doesn't go away; a "scratch" that persists; any lesion that is changing (size, color, shape); may be tender, crusting or bleeding.
  • Shared major risk factor = UV exposure → counsel: limit sun, protective clothing, sunscreen.
Q2. Basal cell carcinoma: who, what does it look like, and what gene?
  • Most common skin cancer; arises from basal keratinocytes (or immature follicle cells). Head and neck of adults.
  • Behavior: slow-growing, locally destructive ("rodent ulcer" that keeps eating tissue), rarely metastasizes → early excision limits disfigurement.
  • Risk factors: all forms of sun exposure (chronic, intermittent sunburns, tanning beds; UVB most damaging), latency 15–20 years, family history, environmental toxins, radiation, xeroderma pigmentosum, immunosuppression. Often multifocal in sun-damaged skin.
  • Gross: pearly pink papule with rolled border, often with central ulceration (e.g., lower-lip lesion); a pigmented variant can look dark (e.g., cheek beside the nose).
  • Micro:
    • Nests / trabeculae of dark-blue basaloid cells (high N:C ratio, scant cytoplasm) that look like normal basal cells.
    • Nests connected to the epidermis, dropping into the upper dermis.
    • Peripheral palisading (cells line up at the edge of each nest).
    • Retraction clefting between nests and the surrounding fibrous stroma.
  • Molecular: inactivation of PTCH1 (tumor suppressor) → constitutive Hedgehog pathway.
    • Germline PTCH1 → nevoid BCC (Gorlin) syndrome: many BCCs at a young age.

Pattern to own: sun exposure + small head/neck lesion + basaloid nests with palisading = BCC.

CheckWhat is the name for the nuclei lining up like a picket fence at the edge of a tumor nest?
Peripheral palisading → basal cell carcinoma.
Step 1 HY
  • Advanced BCC → Hedgehog inhibitor vismodegib (blocks Smoothened).
  • Gorlin syndrome = multiple BCCs + odontogenic jaw keratocysts + palmar pits.
  • Classic sites: BCC on the upper lip, SCC on the lower lip (but biopsy decides; the lower-lip lesion in this lab is a BCC).
Step 1 trap

A pigmented BCC can mimic melanoma. Pearly rolled border + slow growth favors BCC; histology (basaloid nests, palisading) settles it.

Buzzwords
"pearly papule, rolled border" → BCC"rodent ulcer" → BCC"peripheral palisading" → BCC"PTCH1 / Hedgehog" → BCC
Q3. Keratoacanthoma: why is it different from SCC?
  • Low-grade skin malignancy thought to arise from pilosebaceous units; resembles well-differentiated SCC but has a different course and biology.
  • Who / where: sun-exposed skin of men >50, most often the face.
  • Course:
    Rapid growthweeks–months to 1 cm → several cm ("huge")
    →
    Stabilizes
    →
    Regresseswithin ~1 year → residual scar
  • Gross: symmetric dome-shaped nodule with a central keratin-filled crater.
  • Micro: endophytic, crater (cup)-shaped lesion; central keratin plug; well-differentiated squamous cells with glassy pink cytoplasm, minimal atypia, pushing down in tongues and nests but well demarcated (circumscribed); surrounding inflammation.
  • Molecular: HRAS mutations and cyclin D1 overexpression with functional p16 are more frequent than in SCC.
  • Treatment: surgical removal (it can mimic SCC).
CheckA 2-cm crateriform facial nodule appeared over 6 weeks. If left alone, what is the expected natural history?
Growth stabilizes, then regresses within about a year, leaving a scar (keratoacanthoma).
Q4. Squamous cell carcinoma: precursor, in situ, invasive, and risk factors?
  • Actinic keratosis (AK): premalignant lesion on sun-damaged skin, rough "sandpaper" texture.
    • Micro: hyperkeratosis (dense pink keratin; may form a cutaneous horn) + atypia in the lower epidermis.
    • Few AKs progress; treat with cryotherapy.
  • SCC in situ: thick keratin on top with dysplasia underneath involving the full thickness of the epidermis, basement membrane intact.
  • Invasive SCC:
    • Gross: highly variable, from slightly raised red lesion to a large ulcerated red lesion (e.g., dorsum of the hand).
    • Micro: large polygonal cells with abundant pink keratinization forming a mass; tongues and nests infiltrate the dermis with no clear border; normal epidermis alongside; lots of surrounding inflammation.
    • Behavior: 2nd most common skin cancer; older patients; usually localized for years, then enlarges, ulcerates, and can metastasize (rarely). Surgical excision usually curative.
  • Risk factors: sun (UV); carcinogens: tars (polycyclic hydrocarbons), arsenic; chronic ulcers, burn scars; radiation; immunosuppression; AK.
    • Xeroderma pigmentosum (autosomal recessive): defective nucleotide excision repair of UV-induced pyrimidine (thymine) dimers → ~2000× SCC risk, even in childhood.
    • HPV (E6/E7 inactivate p53 and RB) can drive SCC, not only in the cervix.
CheckFull-thickness atypia with an intact basement membrane. AK, SCC in situ or invasive SCC?
SCC in situ. AK = partial-thickness atypia; invasive = breaches the BM.
Step 1 HY
  • SCC arising in a chronic wound or burn scar = Marjolin ulcer.
  • Organ-transplant recipients on immunosuppression → large ↑ in SCC (more than BCC).
  • Histology buzz: keratin pearls and intercellular bridges.
  • UV signature: C→T transitions at dipyrimidine sites, often in TP53.
Step 1 trap

KA vs well-differentiated SCC look alike cell by cell. Architecture decides: KA = symmetric cup with central keratin plug, sharply demarcated, fast growth then regression. SCC = irregular, deep infiltration, no clean border.

Memory tool

SCC risks = "STAR-X": Sun, Tar, Arsenic, Radiation/scars, Xeroderma pigmentosum (+ immunosuppression, HPV).

Q5. Melanoma: how do I spot it clinically and microscopically, and what predicts outcome?

Risk factors

  • UV radiation
  • Family history / genetics
  • Light skin, inability to tan, sunburns easily
  • Many nevi or atypical nevi

ABCDE (gross)

  • Asymmetry
  • irregular Borders
  • variable Color
  • Diameter >6 mm (pencil eraser)
  • Evolution (change over time) = most worrisome

Molecular

  • BRAF (most common), NRAS, KIT
  • Pathogenesis varies by subtype and patient
  • IHC + molecular testing help confirm and classify
Radial growthspreads sideways in epidermis; low metastatic risk
→
Vertical growthnests invade down into dermis → raised nodule
→
Metastasislymph nodes → distant sites
  • Gross: a dark, irregular pigmented lesion, typically excised as a circular piece with a wide margin.
  • Micro: nests of large atypical melanocytes (polygonal or spindle) with pleomorphic nuclei and prominent nucleoli, infiltrating down (vertical phase); surrounding lymphocytes (rarely effective on their own).
    • Pigment varies: abundant brown melanin in some, almost none in others (amelanotic), even within one lesion → the color variation that separates melanoma from a benign nevus.
  • Prognosis: depth of invasion (thickness) = most important; also mitotic rate, ulceration, margins. T1 (<1 mm) does better.
  • Treatment: complete surgical excision (early = dramatically better); sentinel lymph node biopsy (early metastasis); biologics / systemic and targeted therapies for specific drivers.
CheckA melanoma that was flat for years becomes a raised nodule. What changed, and why does it matter?
It entered the vertical growth phase (dermal invasion) → greater depth → metastatic potential and worse prognosis.
Step 1 HY
  • Depth = Breslow thickness (the single best prognostic factor).
  • BRAF V600E → vemurafenib / dabrafenib (+ MEK inhibitor); checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1, anti-CTLA-4) for advanced disease.
  • IHC: S-100, HMB-45, Melan-A, SOX10.
  • Familial melanoma / dysplastic nevus syndrome → CDKN2A (p16).
Step 1 trap

No pigment does not mean benign. Amelanotic melanoma looks pink and can be missed; large pleomorphic cells with prominent nucleoli still say melanoma → confirm with S-100 / HMB-45.

Buzzwords
"changing mole" → melanoma"vertical growth phase" → metastatic potential"Breslow depth" → prognosis"BRAF V600E" → melanoma"S-100 / HMB-45" → melanocytic

ApplyLO 4 application questions

A1A 70-year-old farmer has a slowly enlarging lower-lip lesion with a pearly, pink border and ulcerated center. Biopsy shows basaloid nests with palisading. Should you worry most about metastasis or local destruction?
Local destruction. BCC rarely metastasizes but keeps infiltrating ("rodent ulcer"), so early excision limits disfigurement.
A2A 9-year-old with severe photosensitivity, freckling and two facial SCCs. What DNA repair process is broken?
Nucleotide excision repair (xeroderma pigmentosum) → cannot remove UV pyrimidine dimers → ~2000× SCC risk.
A3A rough, sandpaper-like patch on a bald scalp shows thick keratin with atypia limited to the lower epidermis. Name it and its usual treatment.
Actinic keratosis; cryotherapy. Partial-thickness atypia = premalignant; few progress to SCC.
A4Two melanomas are both 4 mm wide. One is 0.6 mm deep; the other is 3 mm deep with ulceration. Which has the worse prognosis, and what staging step follows excision?
The 3-mm ulcerated lesion; sentinel lymph node biopsy. Depth (thickness) and ulceration drive prognosis; melanoma metastasizes early.
A5An older man has a pearly nodule on the nose, a rough scaly forehead patch, and a fast-growing crateriform cheek nodule. Match each.
BCC; actinic keratosis; keratoacanthoma. All UV-driven keratinocyte lesions; biopsy separates KA from invasive SCC.

IDImage ID drillName the diagnosis (and the feature) before you open each card.

1 · Biopsy from a scarring lesion on a young man's back
Severe (nodulocystic) acne vulgaris. Marked acute + chronic inflammation through the dermis around a ruptured, plugged follicle.
2 · Itchy red rash on the leg, 2 days after a new cleaning product
Acute eczematous (contact) dermatitis. Red papulovesicular rash with oozing/crust; type IV, 24–72 h.
3 · Name the process at ■
Spongiosis → eczema. Multiple round intraepidermal fluid pools (vesicles), not a single linear cleft.
4 · Biopsy of a silvery plaque: name ▲, ∗ and ◄
Psoriasis. ▲ parakeratosis; ∗ elongated rete ridges (regular acanthosis); ◄ neutrophil collections. Granular layer lost.
5 · Flaccid blister: where is the split (▼)?
Pemphigus vulgaris. Suprabasal acantholytic cleft; basal cells left on the floor ("tombstones").
6 · Direct IF for IgG (◄): pattern and target?
Pemphigus vulgaris. Intercellular, net-like ("chicken-wire") IgG against desmoglein 1/3.
7 · Tense blister, direct IF (▲): pattern and target?
Bullous pemphigoid. Linear IgG/C3 along the BM; anti-BPAG1/2 (hemidesmosomes).
8 · Slow-growing lip lesion; border at ◄
Basal cell carcinoma. Pearly pink rolled border with central ulceration ("rodent ulcer").
9 · Small head/neck lesion: tumor and feature at ▲
Basal cell carcinoma. Basaloid nest attached to the epidermis with peripheral palisading (▲).
10 · Grew to this size in 6 weeks on a 60-year-old's face
Keratoacanthoma. Symmetric dome with central keratin crater; expect stabilization then regression.
11 · Rough sun-damaged patch: ∗, ♦ and the diagnosis
SCC in situ (from actinic keratosis). ∗ hyperkeratosis; ♦ full-thickness atypia; BM intact (◄).
12 · Elderly man, years of sun and industrial exposure
Squamous cell carcinoma. Ulcerated red lesion on the dorsal hand; UV + carcinogens.
13 · Low power; ▼ marks normal epidermis. Lesion at ▲?
Invasive well-differentiated SCC. Pink keratinizing tongues/nests infiltrating dermis with no clear border.
14 · Circular excision with a wide margin
Melanoma. Asymmetry, irregular border, variable color; excised with wide margin; depth sets prognosis.

MCQPractice questionsClick an answer to see the explanation.

Score: 0 / 0

1A 24-year-old woman develops an intensely itchy, oozing rash on her earlobes 2 days after wearing new costume earrings. Biopsy shows edema fluid between keratinocytes forming multiple small intraepidermal vesicles and a dermal infiltrate of lymphocytes. Which mechanism best explains this reaction?

C. Allergic contact dermatitis (nickel) is type IV: memory CD4 T cells recruited 24–72 h after re-exposure; histology = spongiosis. A: type I is immediate (minutes) and gives urticaria. B: anti-desmoglein IgG = pemphigus (acantholysis, not spongiosis). D: type III = vasculitis. E: granular IgA = dermatitis herpetiformis.

2A 35-year-old man has well-demarcated plaques with thick silvery scale on his elbows and knees, and pitting of his fingernails. Removing a scale causes pinpoint bleeding. Which biopsy finding is expected?

A. Psoriasis: parakeratosis, Munro microabscesses (neutrophils), regular acanthosis with long rete, dilated papillary capillaries (Auspitz sign). D is backwards: the granular layer is thinned or lost. B = pemphigus vulgaris; C = BCC; E = bullous pemphigoid.

3A 4-year-old with asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis has chronically dry, itchy, thickened patches in the antecubital and popliteal creases. A loss-of-function mutation in which protein most likely predisposes him to this skin condition?

E. Atopic dermatitis (atopic triad, flexural distribution in a child) is linked to filaggrin mutations → barrier dysfunction. A: autoantibody target in pemphigus, not an inherited defect here. B: BP antigen. C: BCC / Gorlin. D: albinism.

4A 19-year-old woman has severe nodulocystic acne with scarring that failed topical retinoids and oral antibiotics. Before starting the next drug, she must enroll in a program requiring two forms of contraception and monthly pregnancy tests. Which drug is planned?

B. Isotretinoin (oral retinoid) is used for severe nodulocystic acne and is highly teratogenic. A and C are topical antimicrobials (first-line with a topical retinoid). D: already failed oral antibiotic; teratogenicity program not required (though avoided in pregnancy). E: steroids can worsen acne.

5A 54-year-old woman has had painful oral erosions for 5 months and now has fragile blisters that rupture into crusted erosions on her scalp and trunk. Gentle lateral pressure on normal-appearing skin causes it to shear off. Which direct immunofluorescence pattern is expected?

D. Pemphigus vulgaris (oral first, flaccid bullae, Nikolsky +): IgG against desmogleins → intercellular "chicken-wire" IF. A = bullous pemphigoid. B = dermatitis herpetiformis. C = lupus band. E would not fit an autoantibody disease.

6An 83-year-old man develops intensely pruritic, tense, fluid-filled bullae on his inner thighs and lower abdomen. His oral mucosa is normal and the bullae do not rupture easily. Biopsy shows a subepidermal blister containing eosinophils. Autoantibodies target which structure?

A. Bullous pemphigoid: IgG to BPAG1/BPAG2 in hemidesmosomes → complement → subepidermal split, eosinophils, linear IF. B = pemphigus. C: not a classic autoimmune target. D = epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (deeper, scarring). E = dermatitis herpetiformis (IgA, celiac).

7A 42-year-old man with extensive plaque psoriasis and new DIP-joint arthritis has not improved on topical therapy. He starts a monoclonal antibody aimed at a cytokine that drives keratinocyte hyperproliferation and neutrophil recruitment in psoriatic skin. Which cytokine is the most likely target?

C. Psoriasis is driven by T-cell cytokines TNF, IL-12/23, IL-17 and IFN-γ; anti-IL-17A (secukinumab, ixekizumab) treats skin and joint disease. A and B are Th2 cytokines (atopy, eosinophils). D and E are anti-inflammatory; blocking them would not help.

8A 66-year-old retired lifeguard has a slowly enlarging pearly papule with telangiectasias and a rolled border beside his nose. Biopsy shows nests of dark-blue cells with scant cytoplasm attached to the epidermis, palisading at the periphery and separated from the stroma by clefts. Dysregulation of which pathway is most responsible?

E. Basal cell carcinoma: PTCH1 inactivation → constitutive Hedgehog (treatable with the Smoothened inhibitor vismodegib). A = melanoma. B = keratoacanthoma. C = xeroderma pigmentosum (raises risk but is a repair defect, not the tumor's driver pathway here). D: not the classic BCC pathway.

9A 62-year-old man has a 2-cm dome-shaped nodule on his cheek with a central keratin-filled crater. He says it was not there 7 weeks ago. Biopsy shows a symmetric, well-demarcated cup of well-differentiated squamous cells with glassy pink cytoplasm and a central keratin plug. Without treatment, what is the most likely course?

B. Keratoacanthoma: rapid growth over weeks to months → stabilization → regression within about a year, leaving a scar (usually excised anyway because it mimics SCC). A: describes aggressive carcinoma or melanoma. C and D: different cell lineages. E: KA is defined by its dynamic course.

10An 8-year-old girl has extreme sensitivity to sunlight, heavy freckling, and has already had two squamous cell carcinomas removed from her face. Her parents are unaffected first cousins. Which cellular process is defective?

D. Xeroderma pigmentosum (autosomal recessive; consanguinity): defective nucleotide excision repair of UV-induced thymine dimers → ~2000× SCC risk, starting in childhood. A = Lynch. B = BRCA. C: base excision repair is not the XP defect. E: radiosensitivity syndromes.

11A 47-year-old fair-skinned woman has an excised pigmented lesion that is asymmetric with irregular borders and variable color. Pathology confirms melanoma in the vertical growth phase. Which single feature of the specimen is most important for her prognosis?

A. Thickness (Breslow depth) is the most important prognostic factor, followed by mitotic rate and ulceration; T1 <1 mm does better. B: diameter is a clinical warning sign, not the key prognostic factor. C: amelanotic tumors are not less dangerous. D: a risk factor for getting melanoma, not prognosis. E: the lymphocytic response is rarely effective alone.

12A 72-year-old man has a rough, scaly patch on his forehead. Biopsy shows marked hyperkeratosis forming a small horn and atypical keratinocytes involving the full thickness of the epidermis. The basement membrane is intact and no cells are present in the dermis. What is the diagnosis?

C. Full-thickness atypia with an intact BM = SCC in situ (arising from sun damage/actinic keratosis). A: AK atypia is partial thickness. B requires invasion through the BM. D: crater-shaped, well-differentiated, minimal atypia. E: no atypia; parakeratosis and neutrophils instead.

13A 58-year-old man has metastatic melanoma. Molecular testing of the tumor identifies a valine-to-glutamate substitution at codon 600 of a serine/threonine kinase. Which treatment specifically targets this alteration?

B. BRAF V600E → BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib (or dabrafenib), usually with a MEK inhibitor. A: Hedgehog (BCC). C: BCR-ABL / KIT (KIT-mutant melanoma is less common and not this mutation). D: acne. E: anti-IL-17 for psoriasis.
